description: Six simulated incident case studies built on the same synthetic events (sample-events.json) and raw logs (sample-logs.json). The organisation, people, hosts and findings are fictitious. Analyst roles are generic; no real persons are named.

priorityMatrix.note: Example impact × urgency matrix. Each organisation defines its own criteria.
impact: 1 · Minor: single user or system, no sensitive data
2 · Significant: multiple systems or sensitive data at risk
3 · Severe: critical systems or confirmed data loss
urgency: 2 · Medium: activity possible or spreading slowly
3 · High: active attacker or imminent impact

references.title: SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management: A CSF 2.0 Community Profile
Federal Government Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks

incidents.title: Multiple failed authentication attempts
incidents.scenario: A burst of failed network logons against a Finance workstation from an external address, followed hours later by an account lockout.

alert.trigger: 6 failures in 38 s from 203.0.113.45 (sample of 25 in the full log)

timeline.text: First failed logon (4625, LogonType 3) for j.doe from 203.0.113.45
COR-001 alert raised; Tier 1 triage begins
Source IP blocked at the edge firewall; no successful logon found
Precautionary password reset for j.doe
Account lockout (4740) from WS-FIN-014, traced to a cached credential on a mapped drive
Case closed after firewall rule review

investigation.question: Did any attempt succeed?
investigation.finding: No 4624 logon for j.doe from 203.0.113.45. All attempts returned Status 0xC000006D / SubStatus 0xC000006A (bad password for a valid user).

investigation.question: Why could an external address reach a workstation?
investigation.finding: A temporary NAT rule created for a vendor session had not been removed, exposing the workstation's SMB/NTLM authentication to the internet.

investigation.question: Is the later lockout a second attack?
investigation.finding: No. The 4740 caller was WS-FIN-014 itself. A mapped drive cached the pre-reset password, so this was a false positive.

incidents.rootCause: An expired vendor NAT rule exposed a workstation to the internet. The valid username suggests prior reconnaissance, but the password held.
eradication: Confirm no other inbound rules expose workstations
recovery: Reset j.doe's password and clear cached credentials
Unlock the account after the user confirms access
lessons: Time-limit vendor access rules and alert on rules older than their expiry
Account-lockout alerts should check the caller computer before escalating

incidents.title: Suspicious administrator login
incidents.detectionSource: SIEM correlation rule COR-002 (success after failures)
incidents.scenario: A privileged service account logged on interactively to a domain controller from a new external address outside any change window. Afterwards the audit log was cleared and a new domain account was created.

alert.rule: COR-002 Successful logon after repeated failures
alert.trigger: 3 failures then RDP logon (LogonType 10) for adm.svc from 192.0.2.77

timeline.text: Password-spraying pattern against 41 accounts from 198.51.100.23 (identity provider)
Three failed logons for adm.svc on DC-01 from 192.0.2.77
Successful RDP logon (4624, type 10); COR-002 alert
Special privileges assigned (4672): SeDebugPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeRestorePrivilege
Security audit log cleared on DC-01 (1102)
New domain account svc_backup2 created by adm.svc (4720)
adm.svc and svc_backup2 disabled; RDP gateway rule withdrawn

investigation.question: Is this logon expected?
investigation.finding: No change ticket covers the logon, adm.svc is a service account that should never log on interactively, and 192.0.2.77 has never been seen before.

investigation.question: How was the credential obtained?
investigation.finding: Assessed with medium confidence: adm.svc was among the accounts targeted by the 22:14 password spray and had a weak, non-expiring password with no MFA.

investigation.question: What did the attacker do with the access?
investigation.finding: Debug and backup privileges were assigned, the Security log was cleared, and a backdoor account svc_backup2 was created. Forwarded logs in the SIEM preserved the events from before the clear.

investigation.question: Is the domain compromised?
investigation.finding: Treated as likely. Domain-wide credential reset is planned, including resetting KRBTGT twice.

incidents.rootCause: A privileged service account with a weak password and no MFA was reachable through an internet-published RDP gateway that forwarded to a domain controller.

evidence.item: SIEM copy of DC-01 Security events (pre-clear)
evidence.integrity: Export SHA-256 recorded in case file
SHA-256 recorded; stored on write-once media

containment: Withdraw the internet-facing RDP gateway rule
eradication: Reset all privileged credentials and KRBTGT (twice, with replication in between)
Review GPOs, scheduled tasks and AD changes made since 22:31
Rebuild DC-01 if integrity cannot be confirmed
recovery: Re-issue service credentials as group-managed service accounts (gMSA)
Restore audit policy and confirm forwarding is healthy
lessons: Service accounts must be denied interactive and RDP logon
Administrative access only from privileged access workstations with phishing-resistant MFA
Log forwarding protected the evidence the attacker tried to destroy; keep it out of reach of domain admins

incidents.title: Suspicious PowerShell execution
incidents.scenario: A Word document on an HR workstation launched hidden, encoded PowerShell that downloaded a payload, established C2, dumped credentials and moved laterally to a file server.

alert.rule: COR-003 Office application spawned a script interpreter
alert.trigger: WINWORD.EXE → powershell.exe -EncodedCommand; script block contains a Net.WebClient download cradle

timeline.text: WINWORD.EXE spawns hidden powershell.exe with an encoded command
Script block shows DownloadString from 198.51.100.88
First outbound TLS connection from PowerShell to 198.51.100.88:443
updchk.exe written to the user's AppData\Roaming
updchk.exe opens lsass.exe (GrantedAccess 0x1010)
RDP logon to FS-02 as m.ito from WS-HR-022
Scheduled task \Microsoft\Windows\UpdateCheck created for persistence
Periodic beacon to 198.51.100.88:443 still observed; host isolated

investigation.question: How did the code start?
investigation.finding: WINWORD.EXE was the parent of powershell.exe, which is consistent with a macro. The lure arrived as a password-protected archive that the mail gateway could not scan.

investigation.question: What did PowerShell do?
investigation.finding: Script block logging decoded the command: an in-memory download-and-execute cradle from 198.51.100.88, followed by a dropped executable updchk.exe.

investigation.question: Were credentials stolen?
investigation.finding: Yes, likely. updchk.exe opened LSASS with read access (0x1010), a common credential-dumping pattern. m.ito's credentials were then used to RDP to FS-02.

investigation.question: Is the attacker persistent?
investigation.finding: A scheduled task disguised as a Windows task was created, and C2 beaconing continued until isolation.

incidents.rootCause: A macro-enabled document inside a password-protected archive bypassed mail filtering. Office was allowed to launch PowerShell, and no ASR rule blocked child processes.

evidence.item: WS-HR-022 memory image and triage collection

evidence.integrity: Hash recorded; stored in malware vault, not detonated outside the lab

containment: Disable m.ito and reset the password; revoke sessions
eradication: Remove the scheduled task and updchk.exe; reimage WS-HR-022
Hunt for updchk.exe and the C2 address across all endpoints
recovery: Restore the user from a clean image
Monitor the account and host for 14 days
lessons: Enable the ASR rule blocking Office from creating child processes
Quarantine password-protected archives from external senders

incidents.title: Possible ransomware execution
incidents.detectionSource: SIEM correlation rule COR-007 + EDR behavioural detection
incidents.scenario: On the file server reached through lateral movement, shadow copies were deleted and thousands of files renamed with a new extension. The EDR isolation command did not take effect straight away.

alert.trigger: vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet (parent C:\Users\Public\svc.exe), then mass file rename

timeline.text: RDP logon to FS-02 with m.ito's credentials (see IR-2026-003)
Shadow copies deleted by svc.exe; COR-007 alert
EDR detects mass rename (3,412 files, .lockd) and requests isolation: status pending_agent_ack
Outbound bulk transfer begins (see IR-2026-006)
On-call engineer shuts the FS-02 switch port after SOC escalation
EDR confirms isolation enforced
Restore from offline backup begins

investigation.question: Is this really ransomware?
investigation.finding: Yes. Recovery was inhibited (shadow copies deleted) and files were renamed in bulk with a new extension by the same unsigned binary in C:\Users\Public.

investigation.question: Why did containment take 28 minutes?
investigation.finding: The EDR agent had lost its connection to the management console, so the isolation command waited for acknowledgement until 00:31. The SOC treated 'isolation requested' as 'isolated'.

investigation.question: What is the blast radius?
investigation.finding: Encryption is limited to FS-02 shares. No other hosts show svc.exe. Offline backups from 21 Nov 20:00 are intact.

incidents.rootCause: Credentials stolen in IR-2026-003 gave RDP access to FS-02. Ransomware ran under that account, and containment was delayed because an isolation request was never confirmed.
containment: Network isolation of FS-02 (switch port shutdown, then EDR isolation)
eradication: Rebuild FS-02 from a clean image
Hunt for svc.exe and its hash across the estate
recovery: Restore shares from the 21 Nov 20:00 offline backup
Validate file integrity with data owners before reopening shares
lessons: Containment is not done until it is verified. Track the isolation status, not the request
Have a network-level fallback (switch, NAC or firewall) when EDR is unreachable
Alert when EDR agents go offline on critical servers

incidents.title: Unusual outbound network traffic
incidents.scenario: An engineering workstation sent a burst of TXT queries with long, base32-looking subdomains to a single domain, from an unsigned binary in a temp folder.

alert.trigger: 7 queries with 32-character labels to cdn-sync.example within 12 s

timeline.text: odsync.exe begins TXT queries to *.cdn-sync.example
COR-005 alert raised
Run key OneDriveSync set to the temp-folder binary (persistence)
WINWORD.EXE spawns rundll32.exe with no arguments
cdn-sync.example sinkholed on internal resolvers

investigation.question: Is the DNS pattern tunnelling or a legitimate service?
investigation.finding: The labels are 32 characters of base32 alphabet, the query type is TXT, the queries come at a fixed rate from one process, and the parent domain is first-seen. This is consistent with DNS-based C2.

investigation.question: Which process is responsible?
investigation.finding: Sysmon 22 attributes the queries to odsync.exe in the user's Temp folder. The binary is unsigned and impersonates OneDrive.

investigation.question: Is there persistence or further execution?
investigation.finding: A Run key launches odsync.exe at logon. A later rundll32 child of Word suggests a second document lure.

incidents.rootCause: Under investigation. Working hypothesis: a malicious document dropped odsync.exe, which uses DNS TXT records for command and control.
containment: Block direct outbound DNS (port 53) except from resolvers
eradication: Remove the Run key and binary; reimage
Retro-hunt DNS logs for the domain and the label pattern
recovery: Return the host after reimage; monitor DNS for 14 days
lessons: Long-label DNS analytics caught what signature tools missed
Force all DNS through monitored resolvers

incidents.title: Potential data exfiltration
incidents.detectionSource: SIEM correlation rule COR-006 (large outbound transfer)
incidents.scenario: While the ransomware host was waiting for isolation, it sent 2.3 GiB over TCP 8443 to an external address. This is consistent with double-extortion data theft.

alert.rule: COR-006 Large outbound transfer to external host
alert.trigger: 2.30 GiB from 10.20.5.14 to 203.0.113.200:8443 over 712 s (baseline about 40 MB per 15 min)

timeline.text: Session from FS-02 to 203.0.113.200:8443 starts (derived from duration)
Session ends: 2,469,606,195 bytes sent; COR-006 alert
FS-02 isolation confirmed
Data-owner review of affected shares begins; legal and DPO engaged

investigation.question: Was data actually sent out?
investigation.finding: Yes. The firewall recorded 2.3 GiB outbound and only 1.8 MB inbound, an upload-shaped session to a first-seen external host on a non-standard port.

investigation.question: Why was this possible during an active incident?
investigation.finding: FS-02 isolation was requested at 00:03:58 but enforced only at 00:31:40. The transfer fits entirely inside that gap.

investigation.question: What data was taken?
investigation.finding: Open. Share access logs and file-server audit data are being reviewed with data owners to determine whether personal data was involved and whether notification is required.

incidents.rootCause: Exfiltration happened in the containment gap described in IR-2026-004. Egress filtering allowed arbitrary outbound TCP 8443 from servers.
containment: Block 203.0.113.200 and restrict server egress to an allow-list
recovery: Notification decision with legal / DPO within regulatory deadlines
lessons: Track containment confirmation, not request time (shared with IR-2026-004)
